summary: This experimental document defines the bundle security protocol for the Delay-Tolerant Networking Bundle Protocol. It provides integrity and confidentiality, with separate protection for the payload and additional data. It also discusses security considerations and policy options.

plainLanguage.summary: The Bundle Security Protocol adds security blocks to bundles carried through delay-tolerant networks. Different block types protect a single hop, the payload, or other bundle blocks.

questions: what is the bundle security protocol
what are bab pib pcb and esb
subtitle: Security blocks for protecting payloads and other data in delay-tolerant bundles.

tldr.problem: Bundles can pass through stressed and partly untrusted networks, so applications may need integrity and confidentiality protections for payloads and other blocks.
tldr.mechanism: The Bundle Security Protocol defines four security block types: BAB, PIB, PCB, and ESB. Ciphersuites specify the algorithms and processing rules for each block.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6257 is an Experimental IRTF document. It defines mandatory ciphersuites but leaves most key management to other mechanisms.

today: RFC 6257 is an Experimental document from the IRTF, published in May 2011. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC describes the work as experimental and for examination and evaluation.

sections.title: Security for Delay-Tolerant Bundles
sections.content:
The Bundle Security Protocol (BSP) provides security features for the Bundle Protocol in delay-tolerant networks. The RFC addresses integrity and confidentiality, and defines separate mechanisms for payload data and other bundle information.

BSP is processed by security-aware nodes. Other nodes can relay security blocks without processing them. A security-source adds a block, and a security-destination processes it; these roles can differ from the bundle's source and destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Some nodes can add or check security blocks, while other nodes simply forward them. Each block identifies which nodes are responsible for its protection.

sections.title: The Four Security Blocks
sections.content:
A Bundle Authentication Block (BAB) protects a single hop between security-aware nodes. A Payload Integrity Block (PIB) protects payload integrity between its security-source and security-destination. A Payload Confidentiality Block (PCB) indicates that the payload has been encrypted.

An Extension Security Block (ESB) protects eligible non-payload blocks. The RFC distinguishes the primary block and payload from other extension blocks, and defines an abstract security block as a way to describe fields shared by the real block types.
sections.plainLanguage: BAB protects one security hop, PIB checks payload integrity, PCB protects payload confidentiality, and ESB applies to other eligible blocks. These blocks have different protection scopes.

sections.title: Processing Order and Security Paths
sections.content:
Security blocks are processed in an order that reflects how protection was applied. A receiving node removes or verifies blocks in the corresponding order, so forwarding nodes preserve the order of blocks they pass along.

The RFC describes how security policies apply at nodes and discusses security paths for different blocks. A bundle can have several blocks with different sources, destinations, and paths through security-aware nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Order matters because each security operation may depend on the bundle as it existed at that step. Nodes preserve block order so later nodes can process the protections correctly.

sections.title: Mandatory Ciphersuites
sections.content:
The RFC defines one mandatory ciphersuite for each of the four block types. They use HMAC for bundle authentication, RSA with SHA-256 for payload integrity, and RSA key transport with AES-GCM for payload confidentiality and extension-block protection.

The document describes required parameters and results for those ciphersuites. Key management is addressed separately; the ciphersuites do not define a complete key distribution system.
sections.plainLanguage: A ciphersuite names the cryptographic methods and rules used by a security block. This RFC defines required choices for each block type, but does not provide a complete method for distributing keys.

sections.title: Security Policy and Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC discusses choices such as whether to sign before or after encrypting, and notes that the primary block remains visible. It describes bundle encapsulation as one option when endpoint identifiers need confidentiality.

Implementations are expected to support BSP and the mandatory ciphersuites to claim full conformance. The RFC also discusses fragmented bundles and the need to reassemble a bundle before some integrity checks can be performed.
sections.plainLanguage: Security policy determines which protections a node adds and checks. Some information, including the primary block, is not encrypted by these mechanisms.
